MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it, so you get a little "lip" you can feel with your fingers or catch with a sock.

It matters more with long tiles like yours. 60 cm porcelain tiles are often very slightly bowed, higher in the middle than at the ends. If you lay them in a brick pattern with each row shifted by half a tile, the high middle of one tile lands next to the low end of the next. To avoid that:

- **Offset rows by a third of a tile (20 cm), not half.** Most manufacturers recommend no more than a third for long tiles.
- **Use tile levelling clips.** They're cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets, and they're very beginner-friendly.

## Grout colour

**Go for a mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile.**

- White or very pale grout looks dirty within weeks on a floor.
- A mid grey hides dirt and still looks neat against pale grey.
- Avoid very dark grout unless you want a bold grid look.

For a bathroom floor, use a stain-resistant or epoxy-modified grout, or seal a standard cement grout once it has cured. It makes cleaning much easier.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Do the floor first, then fit the toilet.** You avoid fiddly cuts around the pan, and you won't have a gap or an untiled patch to deal with if you ever change to a toilet with a different footprint. The toilet then sits on the finished floor. Check the soil pipe still lines up at the new floor height, since tiles plus adhesive add about 10–15 mm.

## How many boxes

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m = 4.32 m² |
| One tile | 0.3 m × 0.6 m = 0.18 m² |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = 24 |
| Plus 10% | 26.4, so 27 tiles |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

**Buy 4 boxes.** Three boxes would be exactly 24 tiles, with nothing spare.

On paper the room fits the tiles perfectly: 4 tiles along the 2.4 m and 6 across the 1.8 m. In practice you'll still need cuts, for three reasons:

- grout gaps push the rows out slightly;
- walls are rarely perfectly square;
- the toilet and any pipes need cutouts.

An offset pattern also creates more cut pieces at the ends of rows. The 5 spare tiles you'll have are a sensible buffer, and it's worth keeping a couple afterwards in case one ever cracks.

**Check that all 4 boxes have the same batch or shade number** on the label. Colour can vary between production runs.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both, just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from around 9 until lunchtime. Sorry about this, especially after you've been so patient with the skip on the drive for the last fortnight. It should be the last noisy bit of the job. Thank you for bearing with us! [Your names]

Adjust the times to suit. Saying when the noise will stop goes a long way with neighbours.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Preparation matters more than the tiling itself.** The floor underneath needs to be solid, clean and flat. Check it with a long spirit level or straight edge. If it's a timber floor, it usually needs overboarding with plywood or tile backer board first, because tiles crack on floors that flex. The videos tend to skip this part.
2. **Dry-lay the tiles before mixing any adhesive.** Lay them out loose to plan where the cuts fall. Aim to avoid thin slivers at the doorway or along the most visible wall. Starting from a centre line, rather than a wall, usually gives balanced cuts at both edges.
3. **Mix small batches of adhesive and check your coverage.** Adhesive starts to skin over in 20–30 minutes, so only spread about a square metre at a time. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile and look at the back: it should be almost fully covered. With large tiles, also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile ("back-buttering"). Hollow spots under a tile are what cause cracks later.

Also, practise a few cuts on a spare tile before cutting real ones. Many hire shops rent wet tile cutters by the day, which makes porcelain much easier to cut.

It's very doable for a first-timer if you take it slowly. Good luck, and enjoy the Saturday.
